Chapter 6. The Road to 1968—A Reluctant Candidacy.
Sometimes, it feels like the world just knows who it needs, even if that person isn’t sure they’re ready to answer the call.
As the 1960s pressed on, America’s wounds only seemed to deepen—Vietnam, racial tensions, poverty, and this growing sense of disillusionment that lingered in the air.
Bobby Kennedy watched it all from the Senate, caught in a tug-of-war between his sense of duty and the pain of reopening old wounds—wounds that were both deeply personal and painfully political.
He didn’t jump at the idea of running for president. Far from it. The memory of his brother’s assassination was still painfully fresh, and the risks to his own family weighed on him every day.
His friends and advisors kept urging him—telling him that his voice was needed now more than ever. But Bobby moved slowly, wrestling with so much doubt. He’d spend long nights talking with Ethel, his wife, and close friends, trying to find some clarity.
The decision didn’t come easy. He worried about splitting the Democratic Party, about the dangers that come with ambition, and about whether he could actually make a real difference.
But the world outside just wouldn’t let him stay on the sidelines. Across America, young people marched against the war, while families mourned sons lost in faraway jungles.
In Memphis, sanitation workers fought for dignity, and in the Mississippi Delta, children were still going hungry. Bobby went to these places. He listened quietly—sometimes moved to tears by what he saw and heard. He felt the pain, the hope, the frustration.
And with every visit, it became harder to just watch from afar.
So, when he finally announced his candidacy in March 1968, he did it with a real sense of gravity. He didn’t promise easy answers—instead, he spoke about shared responsibility.
He called for an end to the war, for racial reconciliation, for a new commitment to justice. The crowds that turned out to hear him weren’t just looking for a politician—they were searching for hope. And in Bobby, they saw someone who truly understood their struggles. Someone who had suffered, and who had changed.
The campaign trail was tough. Bobby went from city to city, shaking hands, listening, and speaking straight from the heart. He was often exhausted, sometimes overwhelmed by all the expectations. But he kept going, fueled by the sense that this was his moment to serve.
The people he met—factory workers, students, mothers, veterans—they became his inspiration. Their stories stuck with him, shaping everything he said and did along the way.
In private, though, Bobby was still haunted by the risks. He knew better than most what public life could cost—especially for a Kennedy. But he also realized that stepping back would mean letting down all the people who believed in him.
So, his campaign became something more than a race for office. It was a kind of pilgrimage—a search for redemption, for meaning, and for a way to help heal a nation that was hurting.
